title: The Hillsborough Disaster
summary: Josh and Chuck cover the Hillsborough disaster of April 15, 1989, when a crowd crush at Hillsborough Stadium in Sheffield during an FA Cup semifinal between Liverpool and Nottingham Forest killed 96 people (97 with a later death). They walk through the crowd control failures at the Leppings Lane end, the opening of an exit gate, the collapse of a crush barrier in Pen 3, and the chaotic emergency response. They then cover the police cover-up and tabloid blame on Liverpool fans (including The Sun), the Taylor Report, the coroner's and inquest outcomes, the 2000 private prosecution, the 2012 Hillsborough Independent Panel, the 2019 retrial and acquittal, David Duckinfield's 2015 admission, the 2025 IOPC report, the Hillsborough Law campaign, and changes to stadium safety such as all-seater stadiums. Includes a listener mail segment and a correction.

segments.title: Introduction
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck introduce the episode on the Hillsborough disaster, written by their UK writer Kyle, and note it was inspired by the earlier Crowd episode.

segments.title: Background and the Leppings Lane entrance
segments.summary: The match setting at Hillsborough Stadium in Sheffield, an FA Cup semifinal between Liverpool and Nottingham Forest. Liverpool fans were allocated the smaller Leppings Lane end, whose narrow street and seven old turnstiles bottlenecked entry, with about ten thousand standing-room fans going into pens.

segments.title: Gate C opened and the tunnel
segments.summary: Police did not direct the outside crowd; around 2:50 pm, an officer asked for a gate to be opened, Duckinfield eventually agreed, and it was opened at 2:52 pm. Crowds flooded into a tunnel leading to already overfull central pens 3 and 4.

segments.title: Crush develops in the pens
segments.summary: Fans were pushed into the packed central pens with no direction from officers. By around 2:55 the situation was clearly wrong, and by about 2:59 a lethal crush had developed; fans climbed fences as the crush worsened.

segments.title: Crush barrier failure and asphyxiation
segments.summary: A crush barrier in Pen 3 gave way, causing a human cascade. The hosts describe how people died of asphyxiation or cardiac arrest in crowd crushes, linking it to the earlier Crowd episode.

segments.title: Photographs and the match stoppage
segments.summary: Photographer David Cannon's disturbing photos of the crush against the fence. Police wanted the game stopped because they thought the surge was triggered by a Liverpool near-goal; a superintendent went onto the pitch to get the referee to stop the match at about 3:06. Officers formed a cordon, and some opened gates while others shoved fans back.

segments.title: Death toll
segments.summary: Ninety-five died on the day with about 700 injured; two more died later, making 97 deaths. Victims included many teenagers, parents, a ten-year-old, and the oldest victim was 67. Tony Bland died in 1993 and Andrew Devine later, with the 97th death recognized in 2021.

segments.title: Public response and Paul McCartney charity single
segments.summary: Immediate public response included a charity single cover of 'Ferry Cross the Mersey' by Paul McCartney and flowers covering the pitch, but public opinion was largely hostile to Liverpool fans.

segments.title: Police cover-up begins and hooliganism narrative
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the police cover-up that blamed drunk, ticketless Liverpool fans, and note a possible hooliganism episode idea.

segments.title: David Duckinfield's unqualified command
segments.summary: Duckinfield was the match commander; he had never inspected the grounds beforehand, was unaccounted for from noon to 2 pm, had never commanded a match at the stadium, and had last worked a match as a patrolman about ten years earlier. He initially claimed Liverpool fans forced the gate open.

segments.title: Cover-up, altered statements, and tabloid coverage
segments.summary: Police altered witness statements and removed unfavorable comments. The British tabloids, including The Sun with its front page 'The Truth', blamed Liverpool fans with false claims; The Sun apologized in 2012 and has been boycotted in Liverpool. The hosts discuss class attitudes of the era.

segments.title: Taylor Report 1990
segments.summary: The 1990 Taylor Report, by Lord Justice Taylor, blamed police failure to control the crowd and Duckinfield for failing to close the central tunnel; it made safety recommendations but did not yet exonerate the victims.

segments.title: Freeman tactic
segments.summary: Closing the central tunnel and opening entrances to less full pens was a known technique, the Freeman tactic, which Duckinfield did not use.

segments.title: Inquests and accidental death verdicts
segments.summary: The inquests returned accidental death verdicts, controversial to families. The coroner excluded evidence after 3 pm, saying victims were dead or brain dead by 3:15, though some survived until about 4 pm.

segments.title: Families' treatment and blood alcohol testing
segments.summary: Families were made to view Polaroid photos of the dead at a gym turned morgue and were not allowed to hold their children. The coroner ordered blood alcohol tests, which showed alcohol was not a major factor.

segments.title: 2000 private prosecution
segments.summary: Families secured a private prosecution. The jury could not reach a verdict on Duckinfield, one deputy was acquitted, and the judge ruled Duckinfield would not face retrial. Charges against Sheffield Wednesday and others were ruled out earlier.

segments.title: 2012 Hillsborough Independent Panel and new inquests
segments.summary: The 2012 Hillsborough Independent Panel released about 450,000 pages; Andy Burnham's role was noted. The new inquests found the 96 victims unlawfully killed, and said 41 might have survived with better rescue.

segments.title: 2019 retrial and acquittals
segments.summary: In 2019 Duckinfield was retried and found not guilty of gross negligence manslaughter, and officers accused of altering reports were also acquitted, leaving no one criminally liable.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Short break between segments.

segments.title: Duckinfield's 2015 admission
segments.summary: After seven days of testimony in 2015, Duckinfield admitted responsibility for the deaths of the 96 and said he froze under pressure, reversing his earlier claims blaming Liverpool fans.

segments.title: Stadium safety changes and the Premier League
segments.summary: The Taylor Report led to all-seater stadiums in top divisions by 1994 and the creation of a sports ground safety authority. Higher ticket prices changed the fan base, and the 1992 Premier League brought big money.

segments.title: Hillsborough Law campaign and IOPC 2025 report
segments.summary: Families are pressing Keir Starmer's Labour government to pass the Hillsborough Law, which would require public officials to tell the truth. The hosts discuss the 2025 IOPC report that found no one would be held responsible, and the sticking point of whether it applies to MI5.

segments.title: Documentaries, photos, and 2012 apology
segments.summary: Chuck recounts seeing the Sports Illustrated photos and a 12-minute Guardian documentary. The hosts mention the 2012 apology by Prime Minister David Cameron for the injustice of blame placed on Liverpool fans.

segments.title: Listener mail: Vincent van Gogh and a correction
segments.summary: A listener (Brian and Alexis) corrects the Van Gogh episode, recommending Loving Vincent. Josh corrects an earlier mistake calling Greece an island.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck sign off with the show's standard closing credits.
